title: Andy Kirk, Pha Terrell, Mary Lou Williams and top 1940s venues; Eddie Vinson
summary: Stephens restarts with Andy Kirk's 1942 visit, Mary Lou Williams at the Coliseum and Gypsy Tea Room, lists the top venues, and praises Eddie Cleanhead Vinson's blues singing.

bands.name: Andy Kirk and His Clouds of Joy

story.theme_name: Medicine shows, minstrels, circuses and the black theater circuit
story.community_name: On the road with minstrel, carnival and tent shows

blocks.x: Well, Ted, you know, we left off talking about moving into a new era into the 70s, 80s, before we got into the 90s, getting a little backdrop on history. A lot of things that we discovered on the tapes that we have been doing. Let's backdrop a little bit. Let's go back to the 40s, back in 1942, when Andy Kirk and his clouds of joy came here with Big June Richmond. And then also one of the singers on the program was a guy by the name of Fay Terrell. Fay Terrell, P-H-A, that's the way he spelled it, was one of the most popular singers of his day. And he made several top recordings on the old Decker labels, if memory served me correctly. And of course, you had people like Mary Lou Williams who came through in 42. And in fact, Mary Lou Williams, she did a special show, I think, at the Coliseum Arena with the backing of Dookie Chase's band. And they also left the Coliseum. And late one night, they went over to the Gypsy Tea Room, a fellow by the name of Louie Messina. Massina, who promoted a lot of boxing fights here in the city of New Orleans, was the general manager and co-owner of the Gypsy Tea Room. That was back in 1942. From then on, the Coliseum Arena, and also, you would say that the Isley Hall in the French Quarter, which is no longer there, it's been toned down. Massina, and also, you could say that the Gypsy Tea Room, Club Rocket, Rhythm Club, the Dew Drop. These were the top venues of the day from the 40s going into the 70s and 80s. A lot of activity was happening then. One of my favorite people was Eddie Cleanhead Vincent when he came here with Cootie Williams. I think, if memory serves me correctly, Eddie Cleanhead Vincent was one of the best repeat blues singers of his time. That is, whenever he would get into the middle structure to repeat a blues phrase to get into the structural embodiment of it, you could just feel it.
